personality_voice.book_baseline: In the books, Voldemort's voice is cold, high-pitched, and deliberate. He speaks in long, controlled sentences that alternate between silky menace and sudden cruelty. He is theatrical and self-aware: he knows he commands fear and uses it consciously. He is contemptuous of weakness, speaks to Wormtail with cutting cruelty that flickers between sadistic amusement and cold dismissal ('Liar,' 'Your devotion is nothing more than cowardice'). He is narcissistic and philosophically articulate — he explains himself, contextualizes his own history, and frames his ambitions as inevitable. At the graveyard, he gives a long, composed speech recounting his own fall and return, relishing the details. He taunts Harry with psychological precision ('obedience is a virtue I need to teach you before you die'), and he is never shrill or frantic — even when surprised by Priori Incantatem, his reaction is described as shocked and 'almost fearful,' but he retains composure in his commands ('Do nothing!'). He also shows a specific kind of dark humor: calling Harry his 'guest of honor,' offering sardonic condolences about Harry's parents, and describing Bertha Jorkins' death with 'cruel amusement.' His voice is the voice of someone who has never needed to raise it.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The film preserves the core vocal register — cold, high, controlled — and Ralph Fiennes renders the hissing quality and deliberate pacing well. Key lines are retained or closely adapted: 'Kill the spare,' 'I could not touch him,' 'I can touch you now,' the Crucio sequences, 'Do nothing! He's mine to finish!' The film Voldemort is recognizably cold, theatrical, and contemptuous. However, the film Voldemort's speech is substantially compressed and loses most of the extended monologue texture. The long graveyard speech — which in the book runs across multiple scenes and includes Voldemort's personal history, his account of surviving as a wraith, his analysis of Harry's protection, his strategic reasoning, and his assessment of each Death Eater — is reduced to a brief address to the Death Eaters ('Thirteen years it's been... I confess myself disappointed') and a short monologue to Harry about Lily's sacrifice. The film also adds lines that have a slightly more performative, almost pantomime-villain tone: 'Attaboy, Harry. Your parents would be proud. Especially your filthy Muggle mother.' This line — particularly 'filthy Muggle mother' — is not book-canon and introduces a cruder register of contempt than the book Voldemort typically uses. In the book, Voldemort's taunts are more psychologically refined; he doesn't resort to slurs so bluntly. The film also omits the cold, deliberate psychological manipulation in the pre-duel exchange and replaces it with more overtly aggressive proclamations ('I'm going to kill you, Harry Potter. I'm going to destroy you').
personality_voice.difference: The main personality traits are preserved: cold voice, theatrical self-presentation, narcissism, cruelty toward Wormtail, contempt for weakness, dark humor. What is lost is the sustained, philosophically articulate register of the book Voldemort — his long, composed speeches that reveal him as a thinker who relishes his own narrative. The film simplifies this into more direct, aggressive proclamations. The added 'filthy Muggle mother' line introduces a blunter cruelty that slightly misrepresents the character's usual style. The book Voldemort's ironic, almost aristocratic condescension is partially flattened into something more conventionally villainous.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The core voice is preserved well enough to avoid a heavy penalty, but the loss of extended monologue texture and the slight shift toward cruder, more aggressive proclamations in the duel represent a meaningful simplification of secondary voice traits. The 'filthy Muggle mother' addition is a small but observable deviation from the book's established register. This places the film in the 18–22 range: main personality preserved, minor simplification of tone and secondary traits.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: In the books (GoF scope), Voldemort functions as the hidden engine of the entire plot. His agency is pervasive even before he appears physically: his plan is the reason the tournament exists as a trap, his instructions drive Barty Crouch Jr., his presence is felt through Harry's scar, his history shapes every political and emotional context. When he physically appears — first as a disembodied voice in the Riddle House, then resurrected at the graveyard — he immediately assumes total dominance of every scene. He controls the pacing of the graveyard sequence entirely: he chooses when to speak, when to torture, when to pause. He explains his own plan to the Death Eaters, delivers his history, assigns blame and reward, and decides to duel Harry 'fairly' — all active choices that drive the scene. His speech to the Death Eaters is a political address. His decision to give Harry back his wand and duel properly is a strategic choice rooted in his need to demonstrate his dominance publicly. His agency is never in doubt.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: The film preserves Voldemort's structural role as the central antagonist and the goal of the whole plot. He appears at the Riddle House (compressed but present), he is resurrected at the graveyard, he addresses the Death Eaters, he duels Harry. His agency is intact in broad terms: he issues commands, he directs the rebirthing ritual, he tortures Harry, he attempts to kill him. The graveyard sequence gives him clear dominance over every other character in the scene.
narrative_role_agency.difference: The primary loss of agency is in the Death Eater address. In the book, Voldemort walks individually to each Death Eater, names them, calls out their failures, assigns them new roles, and delivers a long strategic speech about his plans for reclaiming power (dementors, giants, an army). This extended scene establishes him as a political leader, a strategist, and a ruler who governs through a mixture of terror and reward. In the film, this is drastically compressed: he names a few Death Eaters, delivers one or two lines of disappointment, and moves on. The strategic dimensions — recruiting dementors, recalling giants, positioning himself for a return to power — are entirely absent. His role as a planner and political actor is significantly reduced. Additionally, the Riddle House scene loses the extended dialogue that establishes Voldemort's reasoning about why he needs Harry specifically and why the plan is timed the way it is. This reasoning reveals his intelligence and his strategic patience, both of which are understated in the film.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: The role is preserved and agency is not transferred to another character. Voldemort still drives the graveyard sequence and remains the antagonist. However, the loss of the Death Eater address in its full form means a meaningful reduction in the scope of his agency as a political and strategic actor — not just a threat to Harry, but a leader rebuilding a movement. This compression changes how the character functions narratively. The score falls in the 14–17 range.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Voldemort's motivations in GoF are clearly and extensively articulated. His primary drive is the conquest of death — he explicitly states 'my goal — to conquer death' and describes himself as having 'gone further than anybody along the path that leads to immortality.' His obsession with Harry is not arbitrary: he needs Harry's blood specifically because Lily Potter's protection was channeled through Harry and embedded in Voldemort's own flesh when the curse rebounded. Using Harry's blood means he can now touch Harry and nullify that ancient protection — a strategic necessity he explains in detail. His desire to humiliate Harry publicly (giving him back his wand, insisting on a duel) is rooted in narcissism and a need to demonstrate that his return is absolute and unquestioned. He also reveals a secondary motivation: resentment toward his Muggle father and the circumstances of his birth, which he discusses with Harry at the graveyard. His motivations are layered and internally consistent.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The film preserves the core motivation: he needs Harry's blood to overcome the protection Lily's sacrifice created ('she provided the ultimate protection... It was old magic. Something I should have foreseen'). He also expresses the desire to restore his power and reassert dominance. The explanation of why Harry's blood specifically is required is present, though compressed. The desire to conquer death is not explicitly articulated in the film — it is absent from the graveyard speech entirely. The personal history with his father (standing on his father's grave, the story of his Muggle father abandoning his witch mother) is reduced to a single throwaway line: 'Standing on the bones of my father' — with no elaboration of the revenge narrative or the biographical context the book provides.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The conquest-of-death motivation — which is Voldemort's defining philosophical obsession — is completely absent from the film's graveyard sequence. This is not a compression; the concept is simply not stated. The biographical motivation (revenge on his Muggle father, resentment of his origins) is reduced from a multi-paragraph personal narrative to a single unexplained line. What remains is a simplified 'I want to kill Harry and return to power' motivation, which is correct but shallow compared to the book's layered presentation.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: The surface motivation (Harry's blood, return to power, desire to kill) is present and coherent. But the deepest motivational layer — the philosophical obsession with immortality and the biographical resentment of his origins — is not conveyed. The film's Voldemort wants power and wants Harry dead; the book's Voldemort wants to defeat death itself and has a personal history that explains his particular psychology. This is a meaningful simplification that moves motivations from 'intact' to 'partially flattened.' Score falls in the 8–10 range.

character_arc.book_baseline: Within GoF specifically, Voldemort's arc is a restoration arc: from a disembodied, dependent, weakened state to full physical resurrection and public reassertion of dominance. The book traces this arc carefully: the Riddle House scenes establish his helplessness and dependence on Wormtail, emphasizing how diminished he is ('I am no stronger, and a few days alone would be enough to rob me of the little health I have regained'). The resurrection scene marks the climax of the arc. The Death Eater address is the full expression of his restored authority. The duel with Harry is the first test of his restored power — and the fact that the Priori Incantatem phenomenon forces him to retreat represents a complication: he has returned, but his return is not as clean a triumph as he planned. The arc ends with Voldemort having physically returned but having failed to kill Harry, which sets up the larger arc of the series.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The film traces the same basic arc: helpless voice → resurrection → restored authority → failed duel. The key steps are present. The diminished state is briefly shown in the Riddle House (Voldemort is a voice off-screen, clearly dependent on Wormtail). The resurrection is dramatized faithfully. The Death Eater address exists in compressed form. The duel and its outcome are present.
character_arc.difference: The arc is compressed but structurally intact. The most significant loss is the depth of the 'diminished' starting point: the book extensively establishes just how helpless and humiliated Voldemort is — needing to be fed from Nagini, unable to perform magic, dependent on Wormtail for everything — which makes the restoration more dramatically meaningful. The film's Riddle House scene is very short and does not dwell on this helplessness in the same way. The post-resurrection arc (the Death Eater address as a political reassertion) is also significantly compressed, meaning the 'restored authority' phase is less fully realized. The arc is still recognizable and the key turning points are present.
character_arc.penalty_logic: The arc is compressed but not broken. The key stages exist. The penalty is for the compression of the 'diminished state' phase and the abbreviated 'restored authority' phase, both of which reduce the dramatic weight of the arc without fundamentally altering it. Score falls in the 11–13 range.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Voldemort's two key relationships in GoF are with Wormtail and with Harry. With Wormtail: the book establishes a relationship of absolute power imbalance combined with Voldemort's psychological cruelty. Voldemort knows Wormtail is cowardly, contemptible, and serving out of fear rather than loyalty. He uses this knowledge as a weapon, psychologically torturing Wormtail ('I revolt you. I see you flinch when you look at me') while also granting him rewards (the silver hand) as a tool of control. There is a cold, almost sadistic intimacy to their scenes together: Voldemort sees through Wormtail completely and chooses to articulate it in detail. With Harry: the relationship in GoF is primarily adversarial, but Voldemort's treatment of Harry is theatrically performative — he wants Harry to witness his restoration, wants Harry to be afraid, and wants to kill him in a way that demonstrates his superiority. There is also a thread of connection (twin wands, the scar link) that complicates the dynamic.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The Wormtail relationship is preserved in basic terms: Voldemort is contemptuous, Wormtail is servile, the silver hand reward is present. The Harry relationship is preserved in its adversarial structure. However, the extended Riddle House dialogue — which is where the psychological texture of the Voldemort/Wormtail relationship is most fully developed — is drastically compressed in the film. The film replaces the extended book dialogue (in which Voldemort dissects Wormtail's cowardice at length, accuses him of wanting to desert him, and reveals his own vulnerability by admitting he cannot survive alone) with a brief exchange. The line 'Out of fear, not loyalty. Still, you have proved yourself useful' captures the dynamic in one sentence but loses the extended sadistic intimacy of the book scenes.
key_relationships.difference: The power dynamic is preserved, but the emotional texture of the Voldemort/Wormtail relationship — the sustained psychological cruelty, the near-admission of dependence, the articulation of contempt — is heavily compressed. The book Voldemort's relationship with Wormtail is one of the most revealing windows into his psychology (it shows both his sadism and his vulnerability); the film version reduces it to a conventional master/servant dismissal. The Harry relationship is better preserved.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: The Wormtail relationship loses significant emotional texture without being replaced. The core dynamic is recognizable but the depth is gone. The Harry relationship is mostly intact. This places the score in the 5–6 range — important relationship dynamics are altered or weakened, specifically the Wormtail dynamic which is a primary vehicle for Voldemort's characterization in this book.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: Voldemort's complexity in GoF comes from several sources: (1) His vulnerability — the extended Riddle House scenes show him genuinely helpless, dependent, and aware of it. He admits he cannot survive without Wormtail's care, that he narrowly survived, that he feared he might never return. This is a Voldemort who has been humiliated and nearly destroyed, and who has clawed his way back through sheer will. (2) His self-awareness — he narrates his own history with a kind of dark lucidity, acknowledging mistakes ('I miscalculated, my friends, I admit it') without losing arrogance. He knows he was foolish to overlook Lily's sacrifice, and he says so. (3) His political intelligence — the Death Eater address is a masterclass in manipulation: he controls the room through alternating terror and reward, and his analysis of which Death Eaters stayed loyal and which fled is strategic and precise. (4) His biographical specificity — his father's grave, the story of his origins, the revenge on Tom Riddle Sr., all of which establish him as someone with a particular psychological history, not just an abstract evil force.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The film retains the narcissism, the cold cruelty, the theatricality, and the adversarial relationship with Harry. It preserves the surface of complexity. What it removes: the extended vulnerability of the Riddle House (his near-defeat, his dependence, his fear of non-return); the full Death Eater address with its political manipulation; the biographical narrative (reduced to one unexplained line); the explicit articulation of his conquest-of-death philosophy; the psychological dissection of Wormtail that reveals Voldemort's own self-awareness.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The film Voldemort is recognizable as Voldemort but has been significantly simplified. He is menacing, cold, and theatrical — but the layers that make him a genuinely complex villain (vulnerability, self-awareness, political intelligence, biographical specificity) are largely absent. He functions as an effective antagonist but not as the richly characterized figure of the books. The 'filthy Muggle mother' addition actually works against complexity by substituting a blunt slur for the more psychologically revealing contempt of the book.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: This is a case where the surface is sufficiently faithful to prevent a very low score, but the removal of the complexity layers is significant and systematic. The character has been simplified from a philosophically articulate, self-aware, politically intelligent, and genuinely vulnerable dark lord into a more conventional cinematic villain. This is a noticeable simplification that affects the audience's understanding of who Voldemort is. Score falls in the 8–10 range.

lost_or_transferred_material: Extended Riddle House dialogue establishing Voldemort's helplessness, dependence on Wormtail, and fear of non-survival
Voldemort's explicit articulation of his conquest-of-death philosophy ('my goal — to conquer death')
Extended psychological dissection of Wormtail's cowardice and the sadistic intimacy of their relationship
Full Death Eater address: individual naming, strategic assignments, plans to recruit dementors and giants, political manipulation of the circle
Voldemort's account of his own biography: abandonment by his Muggle father, mother's death, orphanage upbringing, revenge on Tom Riddle Sr.
Voldemort's self-aware acknowledgment of his own mistakes ('I miscalculated... I was foolish to overlook it')
Voldemort's extended account of his survival as a wraith: inhabiting animals, fearing Aurors, the years of waiting
The strategic reasoning behind using Harry specifically, including the detailed explanation of Lily's protection and why his blood nullifies it (compressed in film to brief statement)
Pre-duel psychological manipulation ('obedience is a virtue I need to teach you before you die')
Voldemort's theatrical taunts during the duel, including 'Come out and play... it will be quick... I have never died'
Added film line 'Especially your filthy Muggle mother' — not in books and introduces cruder register than book-canon voice
score_caps_applied: Cap 1 (85): Not triggered — total is below 85.
Cap 3 (75): Not triggered — no major actions transferred to another character.
Cap 4 (70): Not triggered — broad identity is preserved and meaningful characterization remains.
Note: Total of 74 is consistent with the scoring framework given the significant complexity loss and motivational simplification without triggering the more severe caps.
key_observations: The film preserves Voldemort's surface identity faithfully: the cold voice, the theatrical cruelty, the physical description, the narcissism, the adversarial relationship with Harry, and the structural arc of resurrection and failed triumph. Ralph Fiennes' performance captures the deliberate menace of the book character. However, the adaptation systematically removes the layers that make Voldemort genuinely complex in GoF: his vulnerability and dependence in the Riddle House, his philosophically articulate self-presentation, his political intelligence in the Death Eater address, his biographical specificity, and the sadistic intimacy of his relationship with Wormtail. The result is a Voldemort who functions effectively as a cinematic villain but who has been simplified from a richly characterized figure into a more conventional antagonist. The film's graveyard sequence is its strongest Voldemort material and is mostly faithful; the losses are concentrated in the Riddle House scenes and the Death Eater address. The total score of 74 reflects a character who is recognizable and partially faithful but has lost enough defining material to prevent a higher score.
